goals: Move from tactical to strategic thinking across three time horizons.
Tell good costs from bad costs, and use total cost analysis.
Build a balanced scorecard for the supply chain, including sustainability.
Choose and implement supply chain technology step by step, and measure its return.
Explain Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions, reverse logistics and the circular economy.
Lead a high-performing team with clear communication, delegation and structured problem-solving.

handout.intro: This last teaching session brings the whole course together. A supply chain leader sees the whole system, makes decisions that balance cost, service and sustainability, chooses the right technology, and builds a team that keeps improving.

head: Tactical question
Strategic question
rows: How do we move this shipment faster?
What capabilities do we need so speed, cost and reliability come together every year?
How do we cut this cost?
What does this cost protect, and what does cutting it risk?
How do we clear this backlog?
Why do backlogs keep happening, and how do we stop them?

blocks.p: Leaders work on **three horizons at once**: this quarter (keep the operation running), the coming year (build capability and people), and 3–5 years ahead (network, technology and partnerships).
**Scenario thinking** helps: “What if demand grows 20% faster? What if a key supplier region closes? What if same-day delivery becomes normal?”
**Total cost analysis** looks at the whole chain, not one budget line. A cheaper, slower transport mode may raise stock cost, stockouts and customer losses.

head: Good costs (investments)
Bad costs (waste)
rows: Training that cuts picking errors
Rework caused by poor processes
Technology that improves visibility
Express freight caused by poor planning
Preventive maintenance
Old stock caused by forecast errors
Supplier development
Overtime caused by uneven inbound flow

callout.title: A simple rule
callout.text: No cost-cutting proposal is approved without saying **what it protects and what it risks**. Fix the process first; the saving follows.

blocks.p: A **balanced scorecard** looks at performance from four perspectives, so cost is never the only thing that counts. For a supply chain, add **sustainability**.

head: Perspective
Example KPIs
rows: Financial
Total logistics cost, cost per unit shipped, inventory carrying cost
Customer
OTIF, order accuracy, lead time, customer satisfaction (NPS)
Internal process
Throughput, capacity use, dock-to-stock time
Learning and growth
Training hours, staff engagement, improvement projects
Sustainability
CO₂ per unit shipped, packaging waste, share of low-carbon transport

blocks.p: For each KPI write: **target, how it is measured, data source, how often, owner**. Review monthly: look at the three biggest gaps, find the causes, agree actions.

steps: **Define the problem in numbers** (for example: order accuracy 91%, stockouts 18% of items).
**Map the process as it is today** before talking to vendors. Automating a broken process only makes it break faster.
**Evaluate options**: fit to your processes (avoid heavy customisation), connection to your ERP and other systems, vendor references and local support, **total cost over 5–7 years**.
**Implement in phases**: clean the data first, train superusers, run old and new side by side, go live step by step (for example receiving, then picking, then dispatch).
**Measure the return** against the problem you started with.

callout.title: Case: FreshChain
callout.text: A fresh-produce wholesaler used spreadsheets: order accuracy 91%, stockouts on 18% of items, 6% of stock value lost to spoilage each quarter. It chose a cloud WMS first (batch and expiry tracking, FIFO) and delayed route software until the WMS was stable. After 12 months: order accuracy 99.2%, stockouts 4%, spoilage 1.8%. The project paid for itself in 14 months.

blocks.p: **AI and analytics** support decisions; they do not replace them. A model trained on messy data gives confident wrong answers.
The **Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol** groups a company’s emissions into three scopes:

head: Scope
What it covers
Supply chain example
rows: Scope 1
Direct emissions from sources you own
Diesel burned by your own trucks and forklifts
Scope 2
Purchased electricity and energy
Electricity for your warehouse and cold rooms
Scope 3
Everything else in the value chain
Suppliers’ production, transport by carriers, customers’ use, waste

blocks.p: For most companies, **Scope 3 is the largest part**, so the supply chain is where much of the reduction must happen. Practical steps: fuller trucks and better routes, cleaner transport modes, less and lighter packaging, energy-efficient warehouses, and choosing suppliers with lower emissions.

sections.h: 6. Reverse logistics and the circular economy

blocks.p: **Reverse logistics** manages goods coming back: returns, repairs, recalls, reusable pallets and crates, and recycling.

list: **Returns** – check, grade, then re-sell, repair, return to the supplier, recycle or dispose. Fast decisions keep value.
**Recalls** – traceability (batch numbers) lets you find and collect affected products quickly.
**Circular economy** – keep products and materials in use: reduce, reuse, repair, refurbish, recycle.
**Reusable packaging** – crates and pallets that come back and are used again.
**Communication** – a short weekly cross-team meeting: each team shares one success, one problem and one request.
**Delegation** – match the task to the person, explain the goal and limits, support without taking over, review together.
**Structured problem-solving** – define the problem with facts, collect data, find the root cause, test a fix, monitor the result.
**Developing people** – stretch tasks, honest feedback, rotations between functions.
**Trust** – be open about decisions, admit mistakes, share credit.
**Healthy conflict** – disagree about ideas and data, not about people.

sections.h: 8. FLOW and the Six Rights as a leader

head: FLOW
As a leader
rows: Forecast
Build capability before it is needed: people, systems, suppliers
Link
Break silos with shared goals, shared data and shared accountability
Optimize
Make continuous improvement part of daily work
Win
Define success broadly: customers, finances, team, partners and the planet

blocks.p: **Right product. Right place. Right time. Right cost. Right information. Right decision.** The goal is not perfection, but a supply chain that gets better every quarter.

terms.meaning: Linking supply chain decisions to long-term goals, not only today’s problems.
terms.example: Building supplier capacity before demand grows.

terms.meaning: Looking at all the cost effects of a decision across the chain.
terms.example: Slower transport saves freight but adds stock cost.

terms.meaning: Spending caused by waste or failure.
terms.example: Express freight because of late planning.

terms.meaning: A set of KPIs from several perspectives: financial, customer, process, learning (and sustainability).
terms.example: Cost and OTIF reviewed together every month.

terms.meaning: Enterprise resource planning: one system for orders, stock, finance and planning.
terms.example: Sales orders flow from the ERP to the WMS.

terms.meaning: A team member trained in a new system who helps colleagues.
terms.example: Two superusers support the warehouse at go-live.

terms.meaning: Moving and cleaning data from an old system to a new one.
terms.example: A full stock count before the WMS goes live.

terms.meaning: What a project gains compared with what it costs.
Indirect emissions in the value chain, outside the company’s own sites and energy.
Managing products that move back: returns, repairs, recalls, recycling.
Keeping products and materials in use as long as possible.
Giving a task and the authority to do it to a team member.
terms.example: A supervisor leads the cycle-count project.

terms.meaning: A department that works alone without sharing with others.
terms.example: Procurement changes suppliers without telling the warehouse.

quiz.q: Which question is strategic rather than tactical?
options: How do we clear today’s backlog?
What capabilities do we need so backlogs stop happening?
Who is on the night shift?
quiz.why: Strategic questions look at long-term capability, not only today’s task.

options: Express freight because planning was late
quiz.why: Express freight caused by poor planning is waste; the others are investments.

quiz.q: OTIF and customer satisfaction belong to which balanced scorecard perspective?
quiz.why: They measure what the customer experiences.

quiz.q: What should you do BEFORE talking to technology vendors?
options: Map how the process works today and define the problem in numbers
quiz.why: The process map and the problem are the requirements the system must meet.

quiz.q: Why is heavy customisation of a software system a warning sign?
options: It raises cost, delays the project and makes upgrades hard
quiz.why: Every future upgrade must be adapted to the custom code.

quiz.q: Diesel burned by your own delivery trucks is which scope of emissions?
quiz.why: Direct emissions from sources the company owns are Scope 1.

quiz.q: Emissions from your suppliers’ factories are…
quiz.why: Value-chain emissions outside your own operations are Scope 3.

quiz.q: Which is an example of reverse logistics?
options: Collecting returned and damaged products from customers
quiz.why: Reverse logistics moves goods back up the chain.

options: Matching the task to the person, explaining the goal and limits, and supporting them
quiz.why: Clear goals and support build capacity and develop people.

quiz.q: In FLOW, ‘Link’ as a leader means…
options: Breaking silos with shared goals and shared data
quiz.why: Linking connects teams, partners and strategy.
